qs.q: The best screening test for acromegaly is ---
qs.e: IGF-1 level is stable throughout the day and serves as the best initial screening test for acromegaly.

qs.q: Which hormone is most useful for diagnosing acromegaly?
qs.e: IGF-1 is more stable than GH and better reflects long-term GH secretion, making it the preferred screening test for acromegaly.

qs.q: Acromegaly is best confirmed biochemically by
o: IGF-1 and OGTT GH suppression failure
qs.e: IGF-1 is the screening test; failure to suppress GH below 1 ng/mL during OGTT confirms acromegaly.

qs.q: Excess growth hormone after epiphyseal fusion causes acromegaly. Before fusion it causes
qs.e: Pre-fusion GH excess = gigantism. Post-fusion = acromegaly: enlarged hands/feet, prognathism, coarse features, organomegaly. IGF-1 is the best screening test.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acromegaly is excess growth hormone after epiphyseal closure, usually from a pituitary adenoma. It causes insidious skeletal, metabolic, and cardiovascular changes that can be life‑threatening if untreated.

sections.p: Acromegaly is chronic excess of GH after growth plates close, leading to soft tissue swelling and bone overgrowth. Diagnosis requires biochemical proof and imaging.
b: GH > 1.5 ng/mL fasting or failure to suppress GH after oral glucose

t.b: Elevated IGF‑1 confirms GH excess and is the screening test.
Failure to suppress (<1 ng/mL) confirms active GH secretion.
Shows a pituitary adenoma; size guides treatment.

sections.p: Severity is staged by GH/IGF‑1 levels, tumor size, and presence of complications. The most common staging is the Farnsworth system.
b: Stage I: GH < 2.5 ng/mL, IGF‑1 < 1.5× ULN, no complications
Stage II: GH 2.5–5 ng/mL, IGF‑1 1.5–3× ULN, mild complications
Stage III: GH > 5 ng/mL, IGF‑1 > 3× ULN, major complications

sections.p: The majority of cases are due to a GH‑secreting pituitary adenoma. Rare causes include ectopic GHRH secretion and familial syndromes.
b: Pituitary adenoma (benign, <1 cm in most cases)
Ectopic GHRH (e.g., small cell lung cancer)
Familial isolated pituitary adenoma (rare)

sections.p: Symptoms develop slowly over years. Patients report coarse facial features, enlarged hands/feet, joint pain, and metabolic disturbances.
b: Coarsening of facial bones, enlarged hands/feet
Joint pain, carpal tunnel, sleep apnea
Insulin resistance, new‑onset diabetes, hypertension

sections.p: Investigations confirm GH excess, localise the tumour, and assess complications.

t.b: Elevated IGF‑1 is sensitive and specific.
Shows size, invasiveness, and guides surgery.
Detects left ventricular hypertrophy or valve disease.
Common in acromegaly and worsens cardiovascular risk.
Patients may have low bone density despite excess GH.

sections.p: Acromegaly can rapidly progress to life‑threatening complications if untreated.
b: Heart failure, arrhythmias, hypertension
Diabetes mellitus, hyperglycaemia
Sleep apnea, respiratory failure
Aortic stenosis, valvular disease
Colorectal polyps, increased cancer risk

sections.p: Treat the tumour first, then control GH and manage complications. First‑line is transsphenoidal surgery; medical therapy is used when surgery is incomplete or contraindicated.
b: Transsphenoidal surgery – removes tumour, often curative

t.b: They bind somatostatin receptors on tumour cells, lowering GH and IGF‑1.
Used when analogues fail; normalises IGF‑1.
Effective over years but has late toxicity.

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring of GH/IGF‑1, tumour size, and metabolic status is essential. Prevention focuses on early detection and treatment of complications.
b: Annual IGF‑1 and GH testing
MRI every 1–2 years if residual tumour
Screen for diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea
Lifestyle: diet, exercise, smoking cessation

sections.p: Conditions that mimic acromegaly include hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, and skeletal dysplasias.
b: Hypothyroidism – myxedema, weight gain
Cushing syndrome – moon face, truncal obesity
Skeletal dysplasias – congenital bone overgrowth

sections.p: Certain tests can be falsely normal or abnormal in acromegaly.
b: IGF‑1 may be normal in pregnancy or liver disease
GH suppression test can be falsely suppressed by high-dose steroids
MRI may miss microadenomas <5 mm

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of heart failure, new arrhythmia, severe respiratory distress, uncontrolled diabetes, or sudden vision loss

faq.a: GH antagonises insulin action, leading to insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia.
Surgery can cure if the tumour is removed completely; medical therapy controls hormone levels.

faq.q: Is acromegaly common in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: It is rare, but delayed diagnosis can occur; focus on basic biochemical tests and MRI referral.
